analysis.one_liner: Speeds offshore oil-drilling permits and exempts drilling-support vessels from air pollution controls.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by 13 senators including two Democrats, died in the Environment and Public Works Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite how the Clean Air Act applies to oil and gas drilling off the U.S. coast. It would measure air pollution from offshore rigs only by its effect on land, exempt the ships that service rigs from emission control requirements, and force the EPA to decide drilling permit applications within 180 days. It would also strip the EPA's internal appeals board of any authority over those permits and block most delays, leaving court review as the only check. The bill never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Offshore oil and gas companies. Permit decisions would come on a strict 180-day clock, the EPA's appeals board could not revisit them, permits could not be held up by administrative stays for more than 180 days, and vessels servicing the rigs would be exempt from the source's emission control requirements. Compliance costs and legal delay would fall, and drilling projects could move faster.

how_it_helps.text: The EPA would have to take final action on a permit application for offshore exploration within 180 days of filing, with any reconsideration included in that clock.

The EPA's Environmental Appeals Board would have no authority to consider any matter relating to the issuance or denial of an offshore exploration permit, and administrative stays could not extend beyond 180 days after filing.
Air quality impacts of offshore sources would be determined solely by their effects in the corresponding onshore area, narrowing what regulators must consider.

Emissions from vessels servicing an offshore source, including while at the source or within 25 miles of it, would count as direct emissions but would not be subject to any emission control requirement applicable to the source.

analysis.who_pays: People living along the Gulf of Mexico and Alaskan coasts, who would breathe air judged only by onshore modeling while rig-service ships and platforms escape applicable emission controls. The EPA and the public would also lose the administrative appeals process as a check on offshore permits.

drawbacks.text: The bill exempts vessel emissions from the emission control requirements that apply to offshore sources, removing an existing clean-air obligation for ships servicing rigs and platforms.

It eliminates the EPA Environmental Appeals Board's authority over offshore exploration permits, so a company unhappy or a community objecting to a permit decision would have no administrative review, only court.
Measuring air quality impacts 'solely with respect to the impacts in the corresponding onshore area' narrows the analysis regulators must perform before approving offshore drilling.
A hard 180-day deadline could force rushed permit decisions on complex offshore exploration proposals, whatever the quality of the review.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Faster permitting might have sped up offshore drilling projects and the jobs and production that come with them, which the bill's sponsors emphasized. But the way the bill achieved that speed was by removing checks: no appeals board review, limits on stays, vessels exempt from emission controls, and a narrowed air-quality analysis. The cost fell on air quality near drilling areas and on the public's ability to contest permits, while the benefit went to a concentrated set of offshore operators.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Environment and Public Works Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Sen. Lisa Murkowski introduced the bill on June 16, 2011, joined by 12 cosponsors, including Democrats Mark Begich of Alaska and Mary Landrieu of Louisiana.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the day it was introduced.
No further action was recorded — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the existing Clean Air Act framework for offshore drilling stayed in place: vessels servicing rigs remained subject to applicable emission controls, the EPA's appeals board kept its authority over offshore permits, and coastal communities retained the administrative process for contesting them. Offshore operators did not get the faster permits and reduced obligations the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: EPA authority and coastal air rules

for.name: Sen. Lisa Murkowski
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to speed offshore drilling permits and narrow Clean Air Act requirements for offshore sources.

for.name: 12 Senate cosponsors (10 Republicans, 2 Democrats)
for.role: Senate cosponsors, including Sens. Begich (D-AK) and Landrieu (D-LA)

for.name: Offshore oil and gas industry
for.role: Offshore drillers and service companies operating in the Gulf of Mexico and off Alaska
for.what_they_did: The bill's faster permitting, appeals-board removal, and vessel emissions exemption matched the industry's long-standing push for quicker offshore approvals after the 2010 Deepwater Horizon slowdown.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of jurisdiction, never brought the bill to a markup or vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 13 original sponsors included 11 Republicans and 2 Democrats (Begich of Alaska and Landrieu of Louisiana), but the Democratic-led committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Offshore oil and gas producers and drilling contractors
industries.note: The bill would have given operators 180-day permit deadlines, exempted rig-service vessels from emission controls, and removed the appeals board as an obstacle — faster, cheaper paths to offshore drilling. The costs, in the form of weaker air-quality analysis near coasts, would fall on coastal residents rather than the companies.

The bill would strip the EPA's Environmental Appeals Board of authority over offshore exploration permits and cap administrative stays, shrinking the agency's tools for reviewing offshore air permits. Those tools are the public's main non-court channel for contesting such permits.
